title: Hearts not yet soft?
hook: has the time not come for believers' hearts to humble themselves (57:16)

segments.voice: Yesterday: ma'akum, God is with you, and your line, wherever you are.

There's a story told about a man named Fudayl ibn 'Iyad. In his youth, the story goes, he was a highway robber. One night he was climbing a wall to meet someone he shouldn't, and from a house nearby he heard a voice reciting the Qur'an. One verse, a question. He stopped on the wall and answered it out loud: yes, Lord, the time has come. He climbed down a different man, and the story remembers him afterward as an ascetic and a teacher.
screen: `A ROBBER ON A WALL AT NIGHT.`

segments.voice: Surah Al-Hadid, verse sixteen. Pickthall: "Is not the time ripe for the hearts of those who believe to submit to Allah's reminder and to the truth which is revealed". It opens: alam ya'ni lilladhina amanu an takhsha'a qulubuhum. Notice who's asked. Not unbelievers: those who believe, people who already pray and already know the words. Has the time not come for their hearts to soften? The verb is takhsha'a, from khushu', the humble stillness meant to fill prayer. A heart with khushu' has stopped resisting. Sahih Muslim preserves a striking line from the companion Ibn Mas'ud: between the time they accepted Islam and the time God reproached them with this verse, there were only four years. Four years in, and already the question: have you gotten used to it? The verse warns against hearts that grow hard as time stretches on. Then the next verse offers the turn: know that God brings the earth back to life after its death. A dead field after rain. Commentators read the two together: hardness isn't permanent, and a heart can be revived the way the ground is. Read that way, the Fudayl story, whatever its historical details, is the next verse acted out: a hard heart turned over in one night. And the question has no date written on it. It stays open, for whoever hears it.
screen: `ASKED OF THOSE WHO BELIEVE.` · `KHUSHU': A HEART THAT STOPS RESISTING.` · `ONLY FOUR YEARS IN.` · `THE EARTH REVIVED AFTER ITS DEATH.`

segments.voice: Notice where you hold tension, jaw, shoulders, hands, and let it soften. Then hold one place your heart has gone hard, a grudge, a habit you've stopped noticing, a person you've stopped listening to, without fixing it, and ask quietly: has the time not come? On each out-breath, let a little of it loosen.
Khushu': the humble stillness of a softened heart, which Surah Al-Hadid asks believers whether the time has come to have. Today's word.
Your line: has the time not come? Hard ground comes back after rain. That's day six hundred thirteen.

howItsDone: Muslim preachers and teachers often recite 57:16 as a call to renewed sincerity, and the story of Fudayl ibn 'Iyad's turning is widely told in sermons and books on repentance.

original.note: Arabic: has the time not come for those who believe? ya'ni means it has become time, it is ripe.

chat.says: Who is Al-Hadid asking, 'has the time not come for hearts to soften'?
options: Believers who already pray; Ibn Mas'ud said it came just four years in.
Only unbelievers who had never heard the Qur'an recited before.
People in the far future, near the end of the world.
